name: boot
title: How does Linux boot?
question: The page records the kernel from its very first line. What does it do before a program can run?

stops.note: The kernel's first C function (init/main.c), on the boot CPU: everything else starts here.
The architecture's part: for arch/wasm, memory is what the host gives, and the console is the host's.
The memory allocators take over RAM: from now on, the kernel can allocate.
The scheduler: this code becomes the idle task (swapper), which runs when nothing else can.
Start the first real task, kernel_init (pid 1), and let it run.
pid 1: every built-in subsystem's and driver's init function, in order.
pid 1 becomes a program: exec /init. The kernel is up.

name: hello
title: What happens when a program prints?
question: printf ends in write(1, ...): how do the bytes get from the program to the console?

stops.note: The syscall: the fd (1, the console) turns into the open file, a struct file.
The VFS: is the file open for writing? Then the file's own write: a tty's.
The tty's line discipline: turn "\n" into "\r\n", and pass the bytes to the driver.
The console driver (arch/wasm/kernel/console.c): hand the bytes to the host, which shows them.

name: open-fails
title: Why does open() fail?
question: Opening a file that is not there fails with ENOENT. Where in the kernel is that decided?

stops.note: Opening walks the path, one name at a time, from the root (/) down.
Look each name up in the dentry cache: the kernel's memory of the names it has seen. "tmp" is there.
The last name, "missing", is not in the cache: ask the directory. (With O_CREAT, this is where the file would be made.)
tmpfs keeps all its names in the cache, so the name does not exist: remember that, as a negative dentry (a name without an inode). Opening a name without an inode fails: -ENOENT.

name: read
title: What happens in read()?
question: A program asks for 64 bytes of a file. Which parts of the kernel does that go through?

stops.note: The syscall itself: fdget_pos turns the fd into the open file (a struct file), and the position to read at.
The VFS, the same for every filesystem: is the file open for reading, is the range sane? Then it calls the filesystem's own read_iter.
The page cache: a file's data lives in memory pages. Find the page for the position, and copy from it to the program.

name: sleep
title: Where does the time go when a program sleeps?
question: nanosleep() for 30 ms takes 30 ms, but the kernel works for a tiny part of it. What happens in between?

stops.note: Set a high-resolution timer for 30 ms from now.
Nothing to do until then: give the CPU away. The idle task (swapper) runs, and waits for an interrupt.
30 ms later, the timer's interrupt: wake the sleeper up (it is runnable again).
